messages.subject: Cholesky Question
parts:
Hey everyone,
I just installed NIMBLE today and I plan on trying to code my first model up pretty soon. It's a multivariate spatial model, and I had a few of quick questions regarding that.

1) It's been a while since I used BUGS and I can't find whether this functionality is present there, but suppose I want to have an exponential decay matrix, i.e. Sigma[i,j] = exp(-phi*||d[i] - d[j]||), where phi is a decay parameter, and ||d[i] - d[j]|| is the distance between locations i and j. Can I just write a line of code like say Sigma = exp(-phi*D) where D is the distance matrix? If not, then is it better to code it up element wise in the model itself or should I just write a nimblefunction that takes phi and D as arguments and returns exp(-phi*D) if that's even possible? Example would be something like

expmat <- nimbleFunction( 
       run = function(phi = double(), D = matrix()) { 
              returnType(matrix()) 
              return(exp(-phi*D)) 
})

Also in the manual and in various threads I've seen numbers in the parenthesis in function declarations, so for example in the manual for the timestwo function is

timesTwo <- nimbleFunction( 
  run = function(x = double(0)) { 
    returnType(double(0)) 
    return(2*x)
  }
) 

I was just wondering what that's used for.

2) If I recall correctly, JAGS didn't have a built in Kronecker product function. Am I correct in assuming that if I needed it I'd have to code it up myself? Can I write a nimblefunction to do this? something like

kron <- nimbleFunction( 
  run = function(M1 = matrix(), M2 = matrix()) { 
    returnType(matrix()) 
    return(M1 %x% M2)
  }
) 

3) Rather than use the multivariate normal distribution directly, I want to generate a vector of independent standard normals and then multiply by the cholesky decomposition of the covariance matrix. In situations where the cholesky decomposition fails, will NIMBLE just reject the sample (like Stan) or will it shut down completely (like JAGS and WinBUGS)?

Thanks in advance for all the help

messages.subject: Re: Cholesky Question

On Feb 24, 2017, at 4:31 PM, Martin Flores <pik...@gmail.com> wrote:

Hey everyone,
I just installed NIMBLE today and I plan on trying to code my first model up pretty soon. It's a multivariate spatial model, and I had a few of quick questions regarding that.

1) It's been a while since I used BUGS and I can't find whether this functionality is present there, but suppose I want to have an exponential decay matrix, i.e. Sigma[i,j] = exp(-phi*||d[i] - d[j]||), where phi is a decay parameter, and ||d[i] - d[j]|| is the distance between locations i and j. Can I just write a line of code like say Sigma = exp(-phi*D) where D is the distance matrix? If not, then is it better to code it up element wise in the model itself or should I just write a nimblefunction that takes phi and D as arguments and returns exp(-phi*D) if that's even possible? Example would be something like

expmat <- nimbleFunction( 
       run = function(phi = double(), D = matrix()) { 
              returnType(matrix()) 
              return(exp(-phi*D)) 
})

Also in the manual and in various threads I've seen numbers in the parenthesis in function declarations, so for example in the manual for the timestwo function is

timesTwo <- nimbleFunction( 
  run = function(x = double(0)) { 
    returnType(double(0)) 
    return(2*x)
  }
) 

I was just wondering what that's used for.

In BUGS code for NIMBLE you can directly use 

Sigma[1:d, 1:d] <- exp(-phi * D[1:d, 1:d])

In BUGS code, but not in a nimbleFunction, you need to be explicit about the indices, as shown.  As explained in the manual, you can use expressions like Sigma[,] instead, but then you may need to provide a “dimensions” argument to nimbleModel if the size of Sigma can’t otherwise be deduced.

In the type declarations of a nimbleFunction, the argument to “double” is the number of dimensions, with default of 0.  So for your expmat, you would want phi = double(), D = double(2), returnType(double(2)).  You can see a discussion on our github wiki of expanding / modifying the type declaration system in the future (we realize the potential for confusion): https://github.com/nimble-dev/nimble/wiki/Design-of-type-declarations-and-object-creation, https://github.com/nimble-dev/nimble/wiki/NIMBLE-design-questions

2) If I recall correctly, JAGS didn't have a built in Kronecker product function. Am I correct in assuming that if I needed it I'd have to code it up myself? Can I write a nimblefunction to do this? something like

kron <- nimbleFunction( 
  run = function(M1 = matrix(), M2 = matrix()) { 
    returnType(matrix()) 
    return(M1 %x% M2)
  }
)

Yes you’d have to code that yourself.  Per the manual and above discussion, matrix() is not a valid nimble type declaration.  What you want is double(2).  And I think you’ll have to write a loop to fill in the result.  Something like:

kron <- nimbleFunction(
 run = function(M1 = double(2), M2 = matrix(2)) {
   returnType(double(2))
   ans <- matrix(nrow = dim(M1)[1] * dim(M2)[1], ncol = dim(M1)[2] * dim(M2)[2], init = FALSE) ## init = FALSE will make it more efficient
   for(i in 1: dim(M1)[1]) {
     for(j in 1:dim(M1)[2]) {
       ans[ ((i-1)*dim(M2)[1] + 1):(i*dim(M2)[1]) , ((j-1)*dim(M2)[2] + 1):(j*dim(M2)[2])  ] <- M1[i,j] * M2
  }
  return(ans)
}
) ## Note, I did NOT test that and am writing hastily.  I’m just sketching the idea.

Note that in a coming release we’ll support basic constructions like rep(), c(), matrix with initialization vector, etc. which could be used to construct a Kronecker product and/or write the index ranges differently.

3) Rather than use the multivariate normal distribution directly, I want to generate a vector of independent standard normals and then multiply by the cholesky decomposition of the covariance matrix. In situations where the cholesky decomposition fails, will NIMBLE just reject the sample (like Stan) or will it shut down completely (like JAGS and WinBUGS)?

I am not completely sure what you mean here.  If you *declare* independent standard normals, then they will have independent standard normal densities.  If you want them to follow a multivariate normal, I’m not clear why you wouldn’t declare them that way.  If the model is that they are multivariate normal but you want the MCMC to sample them one element at a time, you can do that by modifying the MCMC configuration: remove the default block sampler on the multivariate normal and add a series of univariate random walk (or other) samplers, one for each element.  See the manual and then let us know if you have further questions.

As a separate topic, if you want different failure behavior than you find, you could write a custom distribution to provide the behavior you want.  E.g. if you want a multivariate normal that has different failure behavior, you could write it and make it return log density of -Inf  to ensure rejection of an MCMC proposal.  See user manual for how to write a custom distribution and use it in BUGS code.
Thanks in advance for all the help

--

messages.subject: Re: Cholesky Question
parts:
Sorry, I meant that instead of declaring an MVN(0, Sigma) distribution directly, I could declare a vector X of standard normals and then just say Y = chol(Sigma)*X to get the desired distribution, although I'm not really sure whether that will make a difference since I don't know what's going on under the hood with NIMBLE. At the moment, I believe it's the more efficient way to do things in Stan, and I think that JAGS uses the cholesky decomposition to compute the inverse anyway which is why I was a bit concerned since small decay parameters can lead to a covariance matrice that is numerically not positive definite, even though theoretically it's guaranteed to be so.

In either case, thanks again for the detailed reply, and I'll let you all know if I run into any more issues

messages.author: dd632bd3bbcdd7e9
messages.subject: Re: Cholesky Question
parts:
Oh, yes you could do that.  If the Y is intended as a multivariate latent state, you would instead be parameterizing it via the independent Xs.

What goes on under the hood in NIMBLE is that the BUGS code declares a graphical (aka hierarchical) model, and an MCMC will use only the nodes necessary for a particular sampler.  The User Manual should give a clearer idea about this.  It relies on common concepts of graphical models.  Calculation of a deterministic node updates its value (e.g. Y in your example), while calculation of a stochastic node updates and returns its log probability (density).  If you want to see what is calculated for the sampler of a particular node or set of nodes, typically it will be what is returned by  model$getDependencies(nodes) where model is your R model object and nodes are the nodes of interest for sampling.  E.g. you could do model$getDependencies(‘X[1:5]’) if you have five X[i] nodes.

When thinking about efficiency, it can be useful to think about how the graph is set up.  When you use a dmnorm (MVN) declaration with a covariance or precision matrix, calculation of the Cholesky is “lifted” to be a separate node in the graph.  This means it will only be recalculated if the covariance or precision matrix is changed.  Otherwise it is effectively cached.  See User Manual section 5.2.10 for more on this topic.

If you do it manually, say Y <- chol(Sigma) %*% X, then every time X changes (e.g. in an MCMC proposal), chol(Sigma) will be recalculated as part of calculating Y.  Hence it could be better to say cholSigma[1:d, 1:d] <- chol(Sigma); Y <- cholSigma %*% X.  That makes a separate node for cholSigma in the graph, hence it will not be recalculated if X is changed.

We’re definitely interested in hearing what works best for your problem, either to the list or just to the developers at nimble...@gmail.com
